interfaces.interface_notes: For the 17Al alloy, increasing aging temperature/time progressively transforms the α matrix into β-Mn; the FCC Cu-rich and BCC phases reported to form between β-Mn interfaces were characterized in the peak-hardness samples (17Al 575 °C/6 h), not in this 550 °C/1 h sample.
interfaces.phase_evolution: General aging sequence for Fe-Mn-Al-Cu low-density steels: α → α + FCC Cu-rich phase → α + α-Mn + β-Mn + BCC phase → β-Mn + BCC phase + FCC Cu-rich phase. For this 17Al 550 °C/1 h sample the transformation is at an early stage (mostly α with grain-boundary β-Mn).

processing_steps.processing_steps_notes: Ingots of nominal Fe-35Mn-xAl-5Cu (at.%, x = 15, 17, 19) produced by melting high-purity (>99.9 %) raw materials in a vacuum induction furnace under an argon atmosphere.
Hot-rolled into plates with a thickness of 4 mm.
Plates cut into 10 × 5 × 2 mm³ samples for hardness and microstructure characterization.
Solution treated at 1100 °C for 10 min under an argon atmosphere, followed by oil quenching (parent process proc_st-1100c-10min-oq).
The solution-treated 17Al sample was aged at 550 °C for 1 h followed by water quenching; this defines the sample's terminal state (Table 3, 550 °C aging row, 1 h column).

measurement_conditions.test_standard: Vickers microhardness, load 9.8 N for 15 s, average of 5 measurements

structures.overall_structure: Solution-treated Fe-35Mn-17Al-5Cu (17Al) alloy consists of a single α (BCC) phase.

phases_present.morphology: precipitated primarily along α grain boundaries (short rod-shaped inside α grains)

structures.overall_structure: After aging at 550 °C for 1 h the 17Al alloy remains predominantly an α (BCC) matrix; only early-stage β-Mn precipitation has occurred, primarily decorating the α grain boundaries, together with fine α-Mn particles. The α→β-Mn transformation is far from complete (the 17Al alloy reaches near-complete transformation only after 6 h at 550 °C).

unmapped_findings: EDS-measured chemical composition of the 17Al (Fe-35Mn-17Al-5Cu) alloy (at.%): Fe 43.2, Mn 34.8, Al 17.0, Cu 5.0 (Table 1).
Solution-treated baseline Vickers hardness of the 17Al alloy (1100 °C/10 min + oil quench, common to all aging temperatures) = 259.8 ± 1.5 HV (Table 3).
Elastic modulus of the 17Al alloy measured through compressive stress-strain curves = 175 GPa (used as E in Eq. (1) for K_IC).
Density of the 17Al alloy measured by the Archimedes method = 6.76 g·cm⁻³ (same value used for this sample's density field).
Phase-evolution sequence during aging of Fe-Mn-Al-Cu low-density steels: α → α + FCC Cu-rich phase → α + α-Mn + β-Mn + BCC phase → β-Mn + BCC phase + FCC Cu-rich phase.

The 17Al alloy shows slowed β-Mn precipitation kinetics with respect to 15Al; its α→β-Mn transformation is complete only after 6 h at 550 °C, and its optimal aging temperature range for ultra-high hardness (>900 HV) is ~550–600 °C.

Data measured on OTHER 17Al samples (NOT this 550 °C/1 h sample) and therefore excluded from this sample's fields: peak Vickers hardness 924.9 ± 25.8 HV (575 °C/6 h); nanoindentation average hardness 11.1 ± 0.6 GPa and β-Mn intrinsic hardness 12.2 ± 0.1 GPa (575 °C/6 h); β-Mn composition Mn 36.2, Al 16.3, Cu 2.6 at.% (hardest 17Al sample); indentation fracture toughness K_IC = 6.6 MPa·m^1/2 (hardest 17Al sample); and the TEM analysis of FCC Cu-rich precipitates at β-Mn interfaces (575 °C/6 h).
